Sizing the Order: Specification, Capacity and Materials

Before you say yes to a big order, you need three sets of numbers: exactly what the buyer wants, how many units your workshop can truly make per day, and how much material the full run will eat. This module builds all three, using one running example: 5,000 packs of plantain chips for a company's end-of-year hampers.

A bulk order is not your normal work made bigger. When an order is 50 or 100 times your usual size, five things change at once: the **materials** you must buy before you earn anything, the **labour hours** at your slowest step, the **space** to store raw materials and finished goods, the **cash** you must spend before the buyer pays, and the **risk** that one mistake is copied into thousands of units. Planning means turning each of these into numbers before you agree to a price or a date.

A bulk order turns your kitchen or workshop into a small production line, so you plan it like one.
Start with a written specification

Most bulk enquiries in Nigeria arrive as a phone call or a WhatsApp voice note: "We need about 5,000 packs of chips before Christmas, what is your price?" That message is missing almost everything you need. Your first job is to turn it into an **order specification sheet**: one page that you and the buyer both agree on, and that every later plan in this course refers back to.
**Product and specification:** exact product, size or weight per unit (for example 100 g), recipe or material, colour, flavour, finish.
**Quantity:** the exact number, and whether the buyer accepts a small plus or minus (for example 5,000 packs, no shortfall accepted).
**Packaging and labelling:** pouch type, the buyer's logo or yours, units per carton, carton markings, any batch code or best-before date.
**Quality standard:** the approved sample both sides keep, and what counts as a defect.
**Delivery:** date, time window, address, who receives, whether one delivery or several.
**Price and payment terms:** unit price, deposit, when the balance is paid and how (bank transfer, Paystack link, Moniepoint).
**Documents:** invoice, delivery note, any regulatory numbers the buyer requires (for packaged food, ask whether they require a NAFDAC registration number).
**Contact and changes:** one named person on each side, and the rule that any change is confirmed in writing.
Ask for the approved sample early

Send three sample units, have the buyer approve one in writing, and keep an identical twin in a sealed, labelled bag at your workshop. This is your golden sample. Every quality check in the run compares against it, and it settles arguments at delivery.
Scaling: what grows, and how fast

Materials grow in a straight line with quantity: 125 times the packs means 125 times the plantain. But some things grow faster than you expect. Storage becomes a real problem, because 5,000 packs fill about 100 cartons. Waste that you ignore in a small batch becomes thousands of naira. And the time at your slowest step, called the **bottleneck**, decides your finishing date, not the hours of your fastest worker.
Worked example: from 40 packs to 5,000 packs

For example, Kemi makes plantain chips in Ibadan. A normal weekend order is 40 packs of 100 g. A company's HR officer asks for 5,000 packs for staff hampers. Her own records show she uses about 0.30 kg of raw plantain and 0.025 litres of frying oil per pack, her fryer produces about 80 packs an hour, and 50 packs fill one carton.
Size ratio: 5,000 divided by 40 = 125 times her normal order.
Raw plantain: 40 packs need 40 x 0.30 = 12 kg. 5,000 packs need 5,000 x 0.30 = 1,500 kg, about one and a half tonnes, before any waste allowance.
Frying oil: 40 x 0.025 = 1 litre, against 5,000 x 0.025 = 125 litres.
Fryer time: 40 packs take 40 / 80 = 0.5 hours. 5,000 packs take 5,000 / 80 = 62.5 hours of frying alone.
Storage: 5,000 / 50 = 100 cartons to keep clean, dry and off the floor until delivery.

The order is not "a busy weekend". It is 62.5 hours of frying, 1.5 tonnes of plantain and 100 cartons of storage. Kemi now knows she must plan days, not hours, and that she needs a clean storage corner before the first carton is sealed.

Questions to send back to the buyer

Reply to the enquiry with questions, not a price. A short WhatsApp message works: thank them, then ask for the exact quantity, the delivery date and address, the packaging they expect, whether they need their branding on the pouch, and their usual payment terms. Watch for fake bulk orders

Be careful with a "bulk order" that asks you to pay a registration fee, buy materials from a supplier they name, or that sends more money than the invoice and asks for a refund of the difference. **Capacity** is the number of good units your workshop can make in a day, day after day, without quality falling. Many producers quote from their best-ever day. That is a trap: long runs bring tired hands, material delays, power cuts and cleaning time. This lesson gives you three numbers to replace guesswork: your **bottleneck rate**, your **sustained daily rate** and the order's **takt time**.
A stopwatch
Timing each step with your phone's stopwatch is the start of honest capacity planning.
Step 1: time every step and find the bottleneck

List the steps of your process in order. Then, on a normal day, use your phone's stopwatch to time how many units each step finishes in one hour with the people normally assigned to it. Time each step at least three times and use the average. The step with the lowest rate per hour is the **bottleneck**. The whole line can never go faster than that step, however hard everyone else works.

Step 2: from best day to sustained rate

Kemi's shift is 8 hours. She spends about 1 hour on setting up, heating oil, cleaning and breaks, so the fryer runs about 7 hours. Her **theoretical best day** is 80 x 7 = 560 packs. Real days are lower. Take your own records of finished, good units for your last 10 full working days and calculate the average. If you have no records, run a trial week and count. The average is your **sustained daily rate**. The lowest day tells you how bad a normal bad day gets.
Worked example: Kemi's sustained rate and takt time

For example, Kemi's notebook shows good packs for her last 10 full days: 520, 470, 455, 500, 430, 480, 460, 440, 470 and 475. The order is 5,000 packs, and she plans to make 2% extra for quality samples and rejects, so 5,100 packs. Her fryer runs 7 hours, which is 420 minutes, a day.
Sustained daily rate: 4,700 / 10 = 470 packs a day. Lowest day: 430.
Sustained rate as a share of the best day: 470 / 560 = about 84%.
Production days needed: 5,100 / 470 = 10.85, so round up to 11 full days.
If the buyer allowed only 10 production days, the required rate would be 5,100 / 10 = 510 packs a day, a gap of 40 packs a day above her sustained rate.
Takt time for 11 days: 5,100 / 11 = about 464 packs a day; 420 minutes / 464 = about 0.9 minutes per pack.
Kemi needs 11 production days at her proven rate. She will plan with 470 a day, not 560, and add buffer days separately. Ten days would require 510 a day, which her records say she cannot hold.
Step 3: takt time, the order's heartbeat

**Takt time** is the available working time divided by the number of units the customer needs in that time. It tells you how often one finished unit must leave the line. In Kemi's case, one pack must come off the sealer about every 0.9 minutes. If any step takes longer than takt time per unit with its current people, that step needs help, a second machine or more hours. You will use takt time again in Module 3 to decide how many people each station needs.
Capacity is about good units

Only count units that pass your quality check. If 20 of 500 packs are underweight or burnt, your capacity that day was 480. Counting rejects as output hides the real rate and makes every later plan too optimistic.
Writing your capacity statement

Finish with one sentence you can say to any buyer: "With my current team and equipment I produce about 470 packs a day, so I can deliver 5,000 packs in 11 production days plus 4 days for checks, buffer and delivery." A statement like this, backed by your records, is far more convincing than "I can do it".
Do not buy capacity with unsafe speed

Pushing the bottleneck harder is where accidents happen. With hot oil, never overfill the pot (keep it no more than about one-third full), never leave it unattended, keep a fire blanket close, and never pour water on an oil fire. A burn or fire on day three destroys the whole plan.

Running out of one small item can stop a bulk run as surely as a broken machine. A missing roll of labels can leave 1,000 sealed packs that cannot be shipped. This lesson shows how to calculate everything the full order needs, buy it in the right amounts, and have it arrive in time without paying for stock that spoils.
A cardboard package
Pouches, labels and cartons are as critical as the main ingredient in a bulk run.
The bill of materials

A **bill of materials (BOM)** lists every material in one unit and how much of it. Build it from your own weighed batches, not from memory. Include packaging and the share of each carton. For a pack of chips the BOM includes raw plantain, oil, salt and seasoning, one printed pouch, one label and one fiftieth of a carton.
Three allowances to add
**Overrun:** extra units you plan to make so that quality samples and rejects do not leave you short. Kemi plans 2%, so 5,100 packs for an order of 5,000.
**Material waste:** loss before a unit exists, such as bruised plantain or trimming. Use your own records; Kemi adds 5% on plantain.
**Packaging spoilage:** pouches lost to bad seals or misprints. Kemi adds 3% on pouches and labels.

Next, subtract what is already in your store and check its condition. Then round up to how suppliers actually sell: pouches in packs of 500, labels in rolls, oil in 25-litre kegs. Finally, ask each supplier for their **lead time**, the days between paying and receiving the goods. Printed pouches with a buyer's logo often take longest because artwork must be approved first.
Worked example: Kemi's material requirements for 5,100 packs

For example, Kemi's BOM per pack is 0.30 kg raw plantain, 0.025 litres oil, 1.5 g salt and seasoning, 1 pouch, 1 label and 1/50 carton. She has no printed pouches in stock and 3 empty cartons she will keep as spares.
Plantain: 5,100 x 0.30 = 1,530 kg, plus 5% waste = 1,530 x 1.05 = 1,606.5 kg. She plans to buy about 1,607 kg.
Oil: 5,100 x 0.025 = 127.5 litres. In 25-litre kegs: 127.5 / 25 = 5.1, so she buys 6 kegs (150 litres).
Salt and seasoning: 5,100 x 1.5 g = 7,650 g, about 7.7 kg.
Pouches and labels: 5,100 x 1.03 = 5,253 each. Sold in packs of 500: 5,253 / 500 = 10.5, so she orders 11 packs = 5,500.
Cartons: 5,000 / 50 = 100 for delivery, plus 5 new spares = 105.

Kemi's purchase list: about 1,607 kg plantain, 6 kegs of oil, about 7.7 kg salt and seasoning, 5,500 pouches, 5,500 labels and 105 cartons. The rounded-up extras (247 pouches, 22.5 litres of oil) are a known cost she will include in her price.
Timing the purchases

Materials split into two kinds. **Long-lead, long-life** items such as printed pouches, labels and cartons should be ordered first, as soon as the deposit arrives and the artwork is approved. **Perishable** items, here plantain, must not all arrive on day one: 1.6 tonnes would ripen and soften before Kemi could fry it. She buys plantain in four lots of about 400 kg, each arriving the day before it is needed, and asks her market supplier to hold the same ripeness each time.

Confirm specification on arrival

When each delivery arrives, check it against your specification before you sign or pay the balance: pouch size and print against the approved artwork, oil keg seals intact, plantain firmness and ripeness. A wrong print found on arrival costs a phone call; found after filling 2,000 pouches, it costs the order.
Store food materials safely

Keep oil and food materials off the floor on pallets or shelves, covered, away from chemicals, fuel and pests, and use the oldest stock first. Store pouches in their sealed cartons until use so the food-contact side stays clean.

Scheduling, Quality Gates and the Money Plan

With the order sized, you now fix dates, protect quality across thousands of units and make sure you can afford the run before the buyer pays. You will build a backward schedule with milestones, design quality gates with a stop rule, and cost the order with a week-by-week cash plan and payment terms.
Backward scheduling: start date, milestones, buffers and the daily tracker
Work backwards from the delivery date to find the latest safe start date
Place milestones at 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of output
Build buffer days into the plan instead of planning to finish exactly on time
Track planned against actual output every day and act on a shortfall early

Most late deliveries are decided on the first day, when the producer starts too late. **Backward scheduling** fixes this. You start from the delivery date and subtract every stage, from the last to the first, until you reach the latest date you can safely begin. Then you place checkpoints along the way so a shortfall shows up while it is still small.
A woman arranging tasks on a large calendar
Working backwards from the delivery date shows the real start date, which is usually earlier than instinct suggests.
The stages, last to first
**Delivery:** the agreed date, including travel time to the buyer.
**Final check and loading:** count cartons, pre-shipment quality check, delivery documents.

**Buffer:** working days kept empty to absorb power cuts, sickness or a bad batch. Many planners hold back 10 to 20% of the production days; choose a figure that matches your own record of disruptions.
**Production:** planned units divided by your sustained daily rate, rounded up.
**First-article run:** a short run to confirm the line matches the golden sample before full speed.
**Materials in:** the latest arrival date for everything needed on day one, which in turn sets each order date from its lead time.

Count **working days**, not calendar days. Decide which days your workshop works (for example Monday to Saturday), and mark public holidays, market days when your supplier is closed, and any family or church commitments you cannot move. A plan that quietly counts Sundays will be two days late before it starts.

Rules for acting on a gap
**Gap under 5% of plan:** recover inside normal hours, for example by reducing changeover or idle time at the bottleneck.
**Gap of 5 to 10%:** add planned extra time at the bottleneck only, within safe working hours.
**Gap over 10%, or buffer half used:** call the buyer the same day with the facts and a revised plan, such as a partial delivery on the date and the rest two days later.
Use the buffer last
Treat buffer days as the buyer's protection, not spare production time. If you plan to use them from the start, you have no protection left when a real problem arrives.

On a small order you check each unit at the end. On a run of 5,000 you cannot, and a problem found at the end may already be inside thousands of units. The answer is **quality gates**: planned checkpoints throughout the run, each with a clear measure, a sample size and a rule for what happens on a fail.
A clipboard for recording checks
A simple check sheet at each gate catches a problem within a few hundred units, not a few thousand.
Five gates for a bulk run
Quality gates through the run
Gate 1: materials received
Gate 2: first article each day
Gate 3: interval checks
Gate 4: end-of-day count
Gate 5: pre-shipment check
Each gate stops a different kind of problem before it travels further down the line.
**Gate 1, materials received:** check each delivery against specification (print, size, seals, freshness) before it enters the store.
**Gate 2, first article each day:** the first units of each day are compared side by side with the golden sample before full speed.
**Gate 3, interval checks:** a small sample is checked at a fixed interval, for example 5 packs every 100 packs.
**Gate 4, end-of-day count:** good units counted, rejects counted and recorded, cartons marked with the date or batch code.
**Gate 5, pre-shipment check:** a sample drawn from different cartons before loading.
Measures that anyone can apply

Each check must be something a trained worker can decide the same way every time. Write the measure and the limit. For Kemi's packs: **weight** on a digital scale, no pack under the 100 g stated on the label (she sets her filling target at 103 g so normal variation stays above 100 g); **seal** with no gaps when gently pulled; **colour** within the light and dark reference chips taped beside the station; **crunch and taste** on one chip per check.
Check your scale every morning

A scale that reads wrong ruins every weight check. Each morning, weigh an object of known weight, such as a sealed 1 kg pack of sugar from a reliable brand or a test weight, and write the reading in the log. If it is off, fix or replace the scale before filling.
The stop rule

Decide in advance what pattern stops the line. Kemi's rule: **if 2 or more of the 5 sampled packs fail any measure, stop that station**, find the cause, fix it, then check the last 100 packs one by one before restarting. Common causes in long runs are a worn sealer element, a new lot of material that behaves differently, oil that needs changing, or a tired worker late in the day. Each needs a different fix, so find the cause before restarting.
Worked example: reading day 4 of the quality log

For example, on day 4 Kemi's team made 480 packs and ran 5 interval checks of 5 packs each. Results: check 1, 0 fails; check 2, 0 fails; check 3, 1 underweight; check 4, 2 underweight; check 5 not yet done. The weigher has changed scoops after lunch.
Packs sampled so far: 4 checks x 5 = 20 packs; fails = 0 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 3.
Sample fail rate: 3 / 20 = 15%, against near zero on days 1 to 3.
Check 4 has 2 fails, so the stop rule applies: sealing and filling stop.
Cause found: the new scoop holds less, so fills average about 99 g.
Fix: return to the marked scoop and re-weigh the last 100 packs one by one; 11 are under 100 g and are opened and refilled.
Log entry: date, time, check number, fails, cause, action, and who approved the restart.
The problem was contained to 100 packs, with 11 refilled, instead of being found at delivery inside thousands of packs. The log also shows the buyer, if asked, that her checks work.
Defect rate and rework allowance

At the end of each day calculate the **defect rate**: rejected units divided by units made. If Kemi rejects 9 of 480 packs, that is 9 / 480 = about 1.9%. Compare it with the 2% overrun she planned in Module 1. If the defect rate stays above the overrun, the plan will run short, so treat it like an output gap and act early.
When a buyer mentions AQL

Large buyers sometimes inspect the finished lot using acceptance sampling by attributes, published as ISO 2859-1, where an acceptance quality limit (AQL) and the lot size set how many units they sample and how many defects they accept. If a buyer names an AQL, ask for their sample size and accept and reject numbers in writing, and run your own Gate 5 the same way before they arrive.
Food hygiene does not slow down for deadlines

Follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food throughout the run: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials. Handwashing, hair covers and clean surfaces are never skipped to save time, and anyone with diarrhoea or vomiting stays away from food handling.

A large order can make a business poorer if it is priced from small-batch costs or a quick discount. Bulk orders bring costs you do not see on a normal week: temporary workers and their training days, extra energy, the rounded-up packaging you must buy, delivery, and money tied up for weeks before the buyer pays. This lesson costs the whole run, then checks whether you can carry it until payment.

Cost the run from your purchase list

Use the quantities you will actually buy, after rounding, not the theoretical amounts. Then add labour for every person and every day, including training days, energy for each production day, delivery, the first-article trial and a **contingency**, a small reserve for surprises. Kemi uses 5% of her direct costs.
Worked example: Kemi's full run cost and price

For example, using approximate Ibadan market prices Kemi gathered herself: plantain about N900 per kg, oil about N75,000 per 25-litre keg, pouches about N60 and labels about N25 each, cartons about N1,500. Labour: 3 regular workers at N6,000 a day for 11 days and 2 temporary workers at N5,000 a day for 13 days (11 plus 2 training days). Gas about N25,000 per production day. Delivery N60,000, trial N20,000.

Materials: plantain 1,607 x 900 = N1,446,300; oil 6 x 75,000 = N450,000; salt and seasoning N40,000; pouches 5,500 x 60 = N330,000; labels 5,500 x 25 = N137,500; cartons 105 x 1,500 = N157,500. Total N2,561,300.
Contingency 5%: N162,215. Full run cost N3,406,515, or about N681 per pack delivered.
At a bulk price of N950 a pack: revenue 5,000 x 950 = N4,750,000; profit N1,343,485, about 28% of revenue.

Kemi's true cost is about N681 per pack, not the roughly N468 per pack that her bill of materials alone suggested (0.30 kg plantain N270, oil N75, seasoning about N8, pouch N60, label N25, carton share N30). N950 leaves a healthy margin. A price of N700, which might have looked generous for a big order, would have left almost nothing.

List every payment out and in, by date, and keep a running balance. The lowest point is your **cash gap**: the money you must find from savings, a loan or better terms.

Cash goes out for weeks before the balance comes in, so the lowest point in the cycle decides whether you can take the order.

With a 40% deposit Kemi must find about **N1,344,300** of her own money for over two weeks (the contingency is not counted here because it may not be spent). Payment terms to ask for
A deposit on order that covers at least the long-lead materials; 40 to 50% is a common request for large custom orders.
The balance on delivery, or within a short, written number of days, not "when we process it".
Payment to your business account by bank transfer or a payment link such as Paystack, with an invoice reference.
A written note that custom-printed packaging already bought is paid for even if the buyer cancels.

Only treat the deposit as received when it shows in your bank or wallet app balance. Fake transfer screenshots and SMS alerts are common. Do not order printed pouches on the strength of a promise or a purchase order alone.

If any one fails, negotiate the date, the price, the deposit or the quantity before you say yes.

Sometimes the order is larger than your sustained capacity can deliver by the date. You have four main levers: **work longer**, **add stations** (equipment and people), **share the work with a partner producer**, or **change the delivery** into parts. Each one changes cost, risk and quality differently, and only the numbers show which one works.

Step 1: size the gap

Required daily output = planned units / production days available. Compare it with your sustained rate. The difference is the gap you must close. Remember the lesson from Module 1: when you speed up the bottleneck, the next slowest step takes over, so test each option against the whole line, not one step.
Worked example: the buyer asks for 8,000 packs by the same date

For example, a week after quoting, the HR officer asks Kemi whether she can supply 8,000 packs instead of 5,000 by 10 December. With a 2% overrun that is 8,160 packs in the same 11 production days. Her line runs 7 productive hours a day, and her sustained output is about 84% of the theoretical best.
Required: 8,160 / 11 = about 742 packs a day, against her sustained 470. Gap: about 272 a day.

Option A, 2 extra fryer hours daily: best 80 x 9 = 720, sustained about 720 x 0.84 = 605. Still short, and 10-hour days for 6 days a week is 60 hours, above the 55-hour weekly level that WHO and ILO link to higher risk of stroke and heart disease. Rejected.
Option B, second fryer only: frying rises to 160 an hour, but sealing at 90 becomes the bottleneck. Best 90 x 7 = 630, sustained about 529. Far short.

Option C, second fryer, second sealer and a third peeler: peeling 180, frying 160, sealing 180, so seasoning at 150 becomes the bottleneck. Best 150 x 7 = 1,050, sustained about 881. Enough, but three new people to train and equipment to buy or hire within days.

Option D, partner producer: Kemi keeps her 5,100-pack plan. A trusted producer with a proven 300 packs a day makes 3,000 packs plus 2%, so 3,060 / 300 = 10.2, which is 11 days. Kemi supplies pouches and labels and inspects.

Option D closes the gap without changing Kemi's proven line, and Option C is the backup. Kemi offers the buyer 8,000 packs using a partner, or 5,000 on 10 December and 3,000 a week later if the buyer prefers her workshop alone to make everything.
Capacity options by gain and risk
Partner producer: big gain, managed risk
Added stations: big gain, high risk
Split delivery: no extra capacity, low risk
Longer hours: small gain, high risk
Risk to quality and people
Capacity gained
The best option adds the most good units for the least new risk to quality, safety and the date.

Notice what the numbers show. Longer hours look free but add the fewest good packs and the most fatigue. Adding one machine alone barely helps, because the bottleneck simply moves. A split delivery adds no capacity at all, but it is often the safest answer when the buyer only needs part of the quantity on the first date, for example for an early event.
Making a partner arrangement work

Choose a partner whose work you have seen, not just heard about. Visit their workshop, watch a batch, and check their hygiene and their own records of daily output. Then put the arrangement in writing, even as a simple signed letter.
**Same specification:** the partner receives a copy of the order specification sheet and a golden sample.
**Controlled packaging:** you supply the printed pouches and labels and count them out, so the buyer's branding is only used for this order.
**Quantity, dates and milestones:** partner's daily target, and when you collect or receive each lot.
**Quality gates:** you or your supervisor check their first article and draw an interval sample from each lot; rejected packs are replaced at their cost.
**Price and payment:** price per accepted pack (for example N720), part paid on start and the rest on acceptance, so your margin is protected.
**Identification:** each carton marked with a partner code so any complaint can be traced.

On those example numbers, Kemi earns N950 - N720 = N230 per partner pack before her own costs of inspection and transport, which she estimates at about N20 a pack. That leaves about N210 a pack, or about N630,000 on 3,000 packs, less than on her own packs but with far less risk.

Some buyers require that they are told when part of an order is made by another producer. Tell the buyer about a partner in your quotation. You stay fully responsible for the quality and the delivery of every pack.

The best time to find a partner producer is between bulk orders. Agree a trial order of a few hundred units, run your gates on it, and keep a short list of producers whose output and hygiene you have checked yourself.

A bulk run is won or lost by the team. Too few people at one station and the line waits; too many at another and you pay for idle hands. Untrained temporary workers can create more rework than output. Exhausted workers make mistakes and get hurt. This lesson shows how to size the crew, prepare new people and lead the run day by day.
A team working together around a table
Each person in the crew needs a clear station, a clear target and a clear quality rule.
Line balancing with takt time

For each station, measure the **work content**: the person-minutes needed to process a fixed number of units, such as 100. Divide it by the takt time for the same 100 units. The answer is how many people that station needs. Stations needing much less than one person can be combined, so one worker covers two light jobs.
Worked example: balancing Kemi's crew

For example, Kemi's target is 470 packs a day in 420 productive minutes, so takt time is 420 / 470 = about 0.89 minutes a pack, or about 89 minutes per 100 packs. From her timings in Module 1, the work content per 100 packs is: peel and slice 100 person-minutes, fry 75, season 40, fill and seal about 67, label and carton 30.
Total work content: 100 + 75 + 40 + 67 + 30 = about 312 person-minutes per 100 packs.
Peel and slice: 100 / 89 = 1.1 people, so 2 people.
Fry: 75 / 89 = 0.8, so 1 person. Fill and seal: 67 / 89 = 0.75, so 1 person.
Season 40 / 89 = 0.45 and label 30 / 89 = 0.34. Combined 70 / 89 = 0.8, so 1 person can do both.
Crew: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5 people, with Kemi supervising and running quality checks.

Kemi moves from six people on five steps to a balanced crew of five. The two peeling places go to her two temporary workers after training, and the experienced staff keep the fryer, the sealer and seasoning with labelling.
Who does what in the run
Kemi: plan, buyer, sign-off
Supervisor: tracker and quality gates
Fryer and sealer: experienced staff
Peelers and packers: trained temporary staff
Experienced people hold the bottleneck and quality-critical stations; temporary staff take the easiest stations to learn.

Check the balance on day one. If work piles up in front of one station while the next station waits, move a person or share a task until the flow is even. A small pile of work in front of the bottleneck is good, because the bottleneck should never stand idle; a growing pile anywhere else means that station is short of hands.
Training temporary workers
Hire early enough to train before production. Kemi budgets 2 paid training days, which is why her costing pays temps for 13 days, not 11.
Show, then do: the new worker watches a full cycle, then works beside an experienced person.
Teach the quality rule for their station using the golden sample, for example the slice thickness gauge.
Sign-off test: the worker produces a set amount, such as 30 plantains sliced, and passes three checks in a row before working alone.
Give hot-oil and knife safety rules on day one; temporary staff do not work the fryer.
Safe hours protect people and quality

A joint WHO and ILO study found that working 55 or more hours a week is linked to an estimated 35% higher risk of stroke and 17% higher risk of dying from ischaemic heart disease, compared with 35 to 40 hours. Kemi's plan of 8-hour shifts, 6 days a week, is 48 hours with one full rest day. Give regular breaks, water and a proper meal break, and rotate people on repetitive tasks.
The kick-off briefing

Before day one, gather the whole crew for 20 minutes. Explain the order size, the delivery date and why it matters; show the golden sample; give each person their station and daily target; explain the quality gates and the stop rule; and name the non-negotiables: hygiene, safety and no shortcuts on checks. Make it clear that anyone who sees a problem must speak up, and that stopping the line for a real defect is praised, not punished.
The daily 10-minute huddle
**Yesterday:** good units against plan, the gap, and the defect rate.
**Problems:** anything that slowed the line or failed a check, and what was done.
**Today:** target, any changes to stations, materials arriving.
**Thanks:** name one specific thing someone did well.

Keep the huddle short and standing, at the same time every morning, next to the tracker chart. When the run ends, pay everyone promptly and as agreed, thank the team specifically, and note which temporary workers you would call again.
Agree pay in writing
Give temporary workers a short written note of the daily rate, hours, training days and when they will be paid. Clear terms prevent disputes in the middle of a run.
People per station = work content divided by takt time; combine light stations.

The order is not finished when the last pack is sealed. You still need a clean handover, payment of the balance, and a review that turns this run into better numbers for the next one. Done well, the records from one bulk order become the evidence that wins the next.
A delivery being handed over at a door
A counted, signed handover protects your payment and closes the order cleanly.
Delivery documents
**Invoice** with the order reference, quantity, unit price, deposit received and balance due, and your account details.
**Delivery note** listing the number of cartons, units per carton and total units, with any batch codes.
**Proof of delivery:** the receiver signs and dates your copy of the delivery note after counting, and writes their name. Take a photo of the signed note and the stacked cartons.
**Retained samples:** keep a few packs from each production day, labelled with the date, in case of a later quality question.

If the buyer agreed to a partial delivery, issue a delivery note for each part and show the running total delivered and outstanding. Count cartons together with the receiver before signing; a dispute about a missing carton is easy to settle at the door and very hard a week later. Send a WhatsApp message the same day with the photo of the signed note and a polite reminder of the balance due date.
The after-action review

Within a week, sit with your supervisor for 45 minutes and answer four questions: **What did we plan? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we do differently next time?** Use the tracker, the quality log and your cash records, not memory.
Worked example: Kemi reviews the 5,000-pack run

For example, Kemi planned 5,100 packs in 11 production days. A power cut on one day cut output to 180 packs, so she used one of her two buffer days for production. Total made: 5,210 packs. Rejected: 98. She delivered 5,000 packs on 10 December.
Good packs: 5,210 - 98 = 5,112. Defect rate: 98 / 5,210 = about 1.9%, inside the 2% overrun.
Production days used: 12. Average good packs a day: 5,112 / 12 = 426.
Without the power-cut day: (5,112 - 180) / 11 = about 448 a day, below the 470 she planned with.
Spare good packs: 5,112 - 5,000 = 112, sold through her normal retail customers.
Cause found for the lower rate: temporary peelers were slower in the first three days than in the sign-off test.

Kemi delivered on time because of the buffer, not because the plan was exact. Next time she will plan with about 450 packs a day, give temps one more training day, and arrange a backup generator or a fryer fuel that does not depend on grid power.

Your bulk readiness portfolio

Buyers who place big orders want proof that you can deliver. Keep a simple folder, printed and as a PDF on your phone, with: your **capacity statement** updated from real runs; a one-page summary of each completed bulk order (product, quantity, dates, on-time result, defect rate) with the buyer's permission to mention them; photos of your line, your quality log and your storage; and your standard bulk terms. If you have not yet completed a bulk order, include the capacity calculation, backward schedule and quality gate plan from this course as evidence that you plan properly.
Ask for a reference while the delivery is fresh

A week after delivery, when the balance is paid, ask the buyer for two or three sentences you may quote, or permission to give their contact to future buyers. Specific words such as "5,000 packs, on time, consistent quality" are worth more than general praise.

Why this matters
A bulk order is not a busy weekend
Materials bought before you earn
Labour hours at your slowest step
Space for stock and cartons
Cash spent before the buyer pays
Risk: one mistake copied many times
When an order is 50 or 100 times your usual size, five things change at once. First, materials you buy before you earn anything.
Second, the labour hours at your slowest step.
Third, the space to store raw materials and finished goods.
Fourth, the cash you spend before the buyer pays.
And fifth, the risk that one mistake is copied into thousands of units. Planning turns each of these into numbers before you agree a price or a date.
Step one
The order specification sheet
Product, size and quantity
Packaging, labelling and quality standard
Delivery date, address and receiver
Price, deposit and payment terms
Documents, one contact, changes in writing
Most bulk enquiries arrive as a call or a WhatsApp voice note, like, we need about 5,000 packs of chips before Christmas, what is your price?
Turn that into a one-page order specification sheet that you and the buyer both agree.
Write the exact product and size, for example 100 g per pack, and the exact quantity.
Write the packaging, the labels, and the quality standard: the approved sample and what counts as a defect.
Write the delivery date, address and who receives.
Write the unit price, the deposit, and when the balance is paid.
Finally, the documents the buyer needs, one named person on each side, and the rule that any change is confirmed in writing.
Reply to the enquiry with questions, not a price. Serious buyers respect this.
Worked example
Kemi: from 40 packs to 5,000
Plan days, not hours. The bottleneck decides your finish date.
5,000 / 40 = 125 times her normal order
Plantain: 5,000 x 0.30 kg = 1,500 kg
Oil: 5,000 x 0.025 = 125 litres
Fryer: 5,000 / 80 = 62.5 hours
Storage: 5,000 / 50 = 100 cartons
For example, Kemi makes plantain chips in Ibadan. A normal weekend order is 40 packs. A company asks for 5,000 packs for staff hampers. That is 125 times her normal order.
She uses about 0.30 kg of raw plantain per pack, so 5,000 packs need 1,500 kg, before any waste.
Frying oil goes from 1 litre to 125 litres.
Her fryer makes about 80 packs an hour, so that is 62.5 hours of frying alone.
And 50 packs fill a carton, so she needs space for 100 cartons, clean, dry and off the floor.
So this is not a busy weekend. Kemi must plan days, not hours.
True capacity
Three numbers replace guesswork
Bottleneck: the slowest step per hour
Sustained daily rate: average of 10 days
Takt time: available time / units needed
Count only good units
Never quote from your best-ever day. Time each step with your phone's stopwatch, three times, and use the average.
The slowest step is the bottleneck. For Kemi, frying at 80 packs an hour sets the pace for the whole line.
Next, average your good units over your last 10 full working days. Kemi's average is 470 packs a day, so 5,100 packs, including 2% extra, need 11 production days.
Takt time is the available time divided by the units needed. For Kemi, one pack must leave the sealer about every 0.9 minutes.
And count only units that pass your quality check. Counting rejects makes every later plan too optimistic.
Three allowances
Add these to your materials
Extra units for samples and rejects. Kemi plans 2%, so 5,100 packs for 5,000.
Loss before a unit exists, like bruised plantain. Kemi adds 5% on plantain.
Pouches lost to bad seals or misprints. Kemi adds 3% on pouches and labels.
Build a bill of materials from your own weighed batches, including packaging. Then add three allowances. Overrun is extra you make so samples and rejects do not leave you short.
Material waste is loss before a unit exists. Kemi adds 5% on plantain, so she buys about 1,607 kg.
Packaging spoilage covers bad seals and misprints. Then round up to how suppliers sell. Kemi orders 11 packs of 500 pouches, which is 5,500.
Purchase timing
What to buy first, what to buy in lots
Order first
Buy in lots
Plantain, perishable
Four lots of about 400 kg
Each the day before use
Long-lead items like printed pouches, labels and cartons are ordered first, as soon as the deposit arrives and the artwork is approved. Printed pouches can take 10 working days.
Perishables must not all arrive on day one. Kemi buys plantain in four lots of about 400 kg, each the day before it is needed.
Check every delivery against your specification before you sign or pay.
Stay safe and honest
Safety and scam checks
Oil pot no more than one-third full
Never leave hot oil unattended
Fire blanket close; no water on oil fire
Food stock off the floor, covered
Confirm payment in your account
Pushing the bottleneck harder is where accidents happen. Keep the oil pot no more than about one-third full, never leave it unattended, keep a fire blanket close, and never pour water on an oil fire.
Keep food materials off the floor and covered.
And never release goods until payment has actually landed in your account, not just a screenshot or SMS alert.
Key points
Remember
Turn every enquiry into a specification sheet
Keep a buyer-approved golden sample
Plan with your sustained rate, not your best day
Add allowances, round up to pack sizes
Order long-lead items first, perishables in lots
To remember. Write the specification sheet and keep a golden sample.
Plan with your sustained rate. Add allowances and round up. Order long-lead items first, perishables in lots.

Why this matters
Late, faulty or unaffordable: plan it out
Most late deliveries start on day one
A fault can hide in thousands of units
A big order can make you poorer
Three plans: dates, quality, cash
Most late deliveries are decided on the first day, when the producer starts too late.
On a run of 5,000, a problem found at the end may already be inside thousands of units.
And a large order can make a business poorer if it is priced from small-batch costs.
So you will build three plans: a backward schedule, quality gates, and a cash plan.
Backward scheduling
Count back from the delivery date
Count working days, not calendar days.
Delivery: Thursday 10 December
Final check and loading: 9 December
Buffer: 7 and 8 December
Production: 11 days from 24 November
First-article run: 23 November
Order pouches by 10 November
Backward scheduling starts from the delivery date and subtracts every stage. For example, Kemi must deliver 5,000 packs of plantain chips on Thursday 10 December.
The day before, she counts cartons, does the final quality check and prepares documents.
Before that, 2 buffer days, kept empty for power cuts, sickness or a bad batch.
Production is 11 working days at her proven rate, so it starts on Tuesday 24 November.
The day before, a short first-article run checks that the line matches the golden sample.
Printed pouches take 10 working days, so they must be ordered by Tuesday 10 November, a full month before delivery.
Count working days only. A plan that quietly counts Sundays is late before it starts.
Daily tracker
Watch the gap every evening
Plan, actual and gap columns
Gap under 5%: recover in normal hours
Gap 5 to 10%: extra time at the bottleneck
Over 10% or buffer half used: call buyer
Put 25, 50, 75 and 100% milestones on a wall sheet, and fill in actual good packs each evening. The gap column is the most important number.
After three days Kemi is 70 packs behind, about 5% of plan. That is easy to recover now.
A bigger gap needs planned extra time at the bottleneck only, within safe working hours.
If the gap passes 10%, or half the buffer is used, call the buyer the same day with the facts and a revised plan.
Buffer days are the buyer's protection. Do not plan to use them.
Quality gates
Five gates through the run
Materials received
First article each day
Interval checks: 5 packs every 100
End-of-day count
Pre-shipment check; hygiene never skipped
Quality gates are planned checkpoints, each with a clear measure and a rule for a fail. Gate 1 checks each delivery against specification.
Gate 2 compares the first units of each day with the golden sample, before full speed.
Gate 3 checks a small sample at a fixed interval, for example 5 packs every 100 packs, for weight, seal, colour and taste.
Gate 4 counts good units and rejects at the end of the day.
Gate 5 draws a sample from different cartons before loading.
And hygiene never slows down for deadlines. Handwashing, hair covers and clean surfaces are never skipped, and anyone with diarrhoea or vomiting stays away from food handling.
Day 4: a scoop that held less
2 or more fails in 5 packs: stop, find the cause, then restart.
Check 4: 2 of 5 packs underweight
Stop filling and sealing
Cause: new scoop, fills about 99 g
Re-weigh the last 100 packs
Refill the 11 under 100 g and log it
Kemi fills to 103 g so normal variation stays above the 100 g on the label. On day 4, check 4 finds 2 of 5 packs underweight.
Her stop rule says: if 2 or more of the 5 sampled packs fail, stop that station.
The cause: the weigher changed scoops after lunch, and the new scoop holds less.
She returns to the marked scoop, re-weighs the last 100 packs, and refills the 11 under 100 g. The problem stayed inside 100 packs, not thousands.

Costing the whole run
For example, Kemi costs her 5,000-pack order at approximate Ibadan market prices.
Materials, as actually bought

Delivery
First-article trial

Now the money. Cost the run from the quantities you will actually buy, after rounding up.
Kemi's materials come to about 2,561,300 naira. Labour, including 2 training days for temporary workers, is 328,000. Gas is 275,000.
Delivery is 60,000 and the trial run 20,000.
Direct cost is 3,244,300 naira. She adds a 5% contingency, so the full cost is about 681 naira per pack.
At a bulk price of 950 naira, profit is about 28% of revenue. A price of 700 would have left almost nothing.
Profit is not cash
List every payment in and out by date. With a 40% deposit, Kemi's lowest balance is about minus 1,344,300 naira.
A 50% deposit cuts the gap by 475,000 naira. Staged payment is another option.
A deposit counts only when it shows in your account. Not a screenshot or SMS alert.
Kemi pays for pouches, plantain and wages for weeks before the balance comes in. List every payment by date. The lowest running balance is your cash gap.
Ask for a bigger deposit, or staged payment, for example 40% on order, 30% when the buyer approves the first-article packs, and 30% on delivery.
And never order printed pouches on a promise. Fake transfer screenshots are common.
Key points
Say yes only when all three work
The schedule fits, with buffer
The price leaves your margin after contingency
You can cover the cash gap
Act on small gaps early
Keep a quality log as evidence
Accept only if the schedule fits with buffer, the price leaves your margin, and you can cover the cash gap. If one fails, negotiate before you say yes.

Why this matters
From plan to finished delivery
Close a capacity gap with numbers
Staff the line using takt time
Lead with huddles and safe hours
Deliver, review and prove it
Sometimes the order is bigger than your sustained capacity. You will test your options with numbers.
You will size your crew so no station waits and no one stands idle.
You will lead the run with a short daily huddle and safe working hours.
And you will deliver, review the run, and keep the evidence that wins the next bulk order.
Worked example
8,000 packs by the same date
Need 742 a day; sustained rate is 470
A: longer hours: about 605, unsafe
B: second fryer only: about 529
C: three new stations: about 881
D: partner makes 3,000 packs
For example, the buyer now asks Kemi for 8,000 packs by the same date. With 2% overrun, that needs about 742 packs a day. Her sustained rate is 470, so the gap is about 272 a day.
Option A, 2 extra fryer hours a day, gives only about 605. And 60 hours a week is above the 55-hour level that WHO and ILO link to higher risk of stroke and heart disease. Rejected.
Option B, a second fryer only, makes sealing the new bottleneck. Only about 529. Far short.
Option C adds a fryer, a sealer and a peeler, giving about 881. Enough, but three new people to train within days.
Option D: Kemi keeps her proven line, and a trusted partner with a proven 300 packs a day makes the other 3,000 packs.
Partner margin
What a partner pack earns Kemi
For example, Kemi pays her partner per accepted pack and inspects every lot.
Buyer pays per pack
Paid to partner per pack
Kemi's inspection and transport
Naira prices are approximate.
Choose a partner whose work you have seen. Visit, watch a batch, check hygiene and their output records, and put it in writing.
The buyer pays 950 naira a pack. Kemi pays her partner 720 per accepted pack, and spends about 20 on inspection and transport.
That leaves about 210 naira a pack, about 630,000 on 3,000 packs. Less than her own packs, but with far less risk.
Give the partner the specification sheet and a golden sample, supply the printed pouches yourself, and tell the buyer about the partner. You stay responsible for every pack.
Line balancing
People per station = work / takt
Experienced staff hold the bottleneck and quality steps.
Takt: about 89 minutes per 100 packs
Peel 100 / 89 = 1.1, so 2 people
Fry 75 / 89 = 0.8, so 1 person
Seal 67 / 89 = 0.75, so 1 person
Season plus label 70 / 89: 1 person
Work content means the person-minutes a station needs for 100 units. Divide it by takt time for 100 units. Kemi's takt is about 89 minutes per 100 packs.
Peeling needs 100 person-minutes, so 1.1 people, rounded up to 2.
Frying and sealing each need 1 person.
Seasoning and labelling are light, so one person does both. That is a crew of 5, with Kemi supervising.
Her two trained temporary workers take the peeling places. Experienced staff keep the fryer and sealer.
Temporary workers
Train and sign off before day one
2 paid training days
Show, then do beside an expert
Teach the quality rule with the sample
Sign-off: three checks passed in a row
Temporary staff do not work the fryer
Untrained workers can create more rework than output. Kemi budgets 2 paid training days. The new worker watches a full cycle, then works beside an experienced person.
She works alone only after passing three checks in a row. Safety rules come on day one, and temporary staff do not work the fryer.
Leading the run
Safe hours, kick-off and huddle
8-hour shifts, 6 days: 48 hours with a full rest day. Breaks, water and a proper meal.
Order, date, golden sample, each station's target, the stop rule, hygiene and safety.
Yesterday's gap and defects, problems, today's target, and thanks to someone.
Exhausted workers make mistakes and get hurt. Kemi plans 48 hours a week with a full rest day, well below 55, and rotates people on repetitive tasks.
Before day one, a 20-minute kick-off. Anyone who sees a problem must speak up, and stopping the line for a real defect is praised, not punished.
Every morning, a standing 10-minute huddle next to the tracker.
Delivery day
Hand over cleanly
Invoice with balance due
Delivery note: cartons and units
Count cartons with the receiver
Signed, dated note, photographed
Retained samples from each day
A missing carton is easy to settle at the door and very hard a week later. Count together, get the delivery note signed and dated, and photograph it with the stacked cartons.
Keep a few packs from each day, and send a WhatsApp the same day with the photo and a reminder of the balance due date.
After-action review
Four questions within a week
Plan the next order with real numbers, not the old plan.
What did we plan?
What actually happened?
Why was there a difference?
What will we do differently?
Within a week, sit with your supervisor and use your records, not memory. Kemi planned 470 good packs a day. Without the power-cut day, she averaged about 448.
Why? Temporary peelers were slower in the first three days. She delivered on time because of the buffer, not because the plan was exact.
Next time she plans with about 450 a day, adds a training day, and arranges backup power.
Key points
Remember
Size the gap, test options on the whole line
A partner needs the same spec and gates
Plan hours well below 55 a week
Get a signed, dated delivery note
Keep a bulk readiness portfolio
To remember. Size the gap and test every option on the whole line. Give partners the same specification and gates. Keep hours safe, and get a signed delivery note.
Then keep a portfolio of real evidence: your capacity statement, order summaries, photos and a buyer reference.
